utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone, both in and just outside the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Mahindaratne, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But prior to commencement of examination, I have been informed by the Defence that -- that they would like to address the issue of the admissibility of some documents, and I think it might be efficient for both parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you. I have some substantial comments on the admissibility of a number of the documents that the Prosecution seeks to adduce through this witness. I also understand that Mr. Mikulicic has some comments, also Mr. Misetic. You know already, I think, Your Honours, that the Cermak Defence team filed three motions last week on Saturday, addressing this particular issue, and I won't rehearse now all of the arguments that we made then, but I will summarize the essence of those arguments. Our objection relates to two categories of documents that the Prosecution seek to bring in through this witness: First of all, a series of MUP Ministry of Interior Official Notes which are in the form of statements of certain witnesses, including one concerning Mr. Cermak; and, secondly, we object specifically - and I think this objection will be unique to us, and it won't be objected to by the other Defence team - to three media articles, which I will deal with finally. The MUP Official Notes first, and if it assists, Mr. President, I can give you the 65 ter numbers of those documents. They are 65 ter 2344, which is an MUP Official Note of Draginja Djuric; 65 ter 3298, relating to an MUP Official Note from Nada Surjak; 65 ter 6085, relating to Veselin Karanovic; 65 ter 6086, relating to Marija Djuric; and, lastly, 65 ter 4388, an MUP Official Note relating to Ivan Cermak. All of those MUP Official Notes are addressed in the written pleadings that we filed on Saturday. We would like to add a further three documents now, orally, to our motion, which address those Official Notes in respect of Nada Surjak, Veselin Karanovic, and Marija Djuric, and they are these: 65 ter 327, relating to MUP Official Note for Zeljko Sacic; 65 ter 2655, relating to Branko Balunovic; 65 ter 326, relating to Mladen Markac. Our grounds and, very briefly, Your Honours, because we argue this matter in the three filings that we made on Saturday, these MUP Official Notes purport to be witness statements. They are, in effect, hearsay, and the ones that I have specifically reference that we object to go to the acts and conduct, or the alleged acts and conduct, of Mr. Cermak. They have no indicia of reliability. They are, in effect, summaries of an interview with a witness made by a Croatian police officer, and it seems that they were made after the event, so after the interview. They are not signed by the witness. They were not taken down by the Croatian police for any form of criminal proceedings. They are not contemporaneous with the events in question, in Grubori. This witness who is coming before you today simply received these documents. He cannot say anything about the truth of the content of these particular notes. They are not formal statements in the sense, as we understand them in this court. Now, in particular, they go, as I have said, to the acts and contact of the accused; and both the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal and also this Trial Chamber in another case has advised extreme caution in admitting out-of-court statements about the acts and conduct of the accused which cannot be tested by the Defence. What I mean by this is the following: We cannot cross-examine this witness on the content of those statements, because he cannot speak to the content of those statements. And if we could, for a moment, Your Honour, please, go into private session, because I want to address a matter which I think absolutely exemplifies what I'm trying to say here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours, in respect of three media articles, 6102, 6103, and 3476. 6102 is an article entitled "Five Chetniks killed." It makes no mention of events in Grubori at all. There are unidentified sources within that document. It characterizes acts and conduct of Mr. Cermak. We cannot cross-examine this witness on the truth of the content of that particular journalistic article, which is full of journalistic comment, and it is very difficult to separate what is possibly attributed to Mr. Cermak and what is journalistic comment. The Prosecution should call, at the very least, the journalist who wrote this article so that we can at least try and get to the bottom of the nature of this article. We make the same comments in respect of 65 ter 6103, and we make the same comments in respect of 3476. If you'd just allow me, Your Honour, one moment to consult with my colleague, but I think I may have finished my submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Markac Defence has notified that it will join the submissions by the Cermak. Mr. Mikulicic, would you like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to add one more aspect, which refers to the Official Notes. As for the formal legal value of Official Notes in Croatia, in criminal proceedings, it will be explained to us by a witness at least in cross-examination, the witness that worked on those issues for a number of years. However, I would like to remind everybody of the practice of this particular Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber has already met with the proposal of introducing Official Notes in evidence, however, when we were faced with an Official Note drafted by the MUP of the Republic of Croatia with respect to the witness was sitting in the courtroom. Then, for procedural matters, the witness would be asked whether the Official Note reflected the contents of the interview with the MUP official. Some witnesses would confirm that that was the case with minor amendments. However, some witnesses, for example, Stjepan Buhin, clearly stated that the Official Note did not reflect the contents of the interview that they had; and in such a situation, the Trial Chamber would disallow the admission of such an Official Note into evidence. Now we are faced with a difference situation. We are dealing with the Official Notes of the persons who will not come to this courtroom as witnesses, who cannot say anything about the veracity of the notes; and the Defence does not have the possibility to cross-examine such witnesses. Thus, the Markac Defence conclusion and proposal is identical to the Cermak Defence, and that is that there is it no grounds for these Official Notes that the OTP proposed to be admitted to, indeed, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would join in my colleagues with respect to notes that go to specifically the acts and conduct of the accused, which I think is particular situation here. This is where we join their objection. I would also like to put on the record that, over the weekend, the Prosecution filed its response to our 92 bis application where it opposed the admission into evidence of a statement taken by the OTP, I think even years before the statements taken that they are trying to admit today that were taken by the MUP. Our position is that the Prosecution cannot have it both ways. A statement taken by Prosecution which the Defence would like to tender through the cross-examination of a witness soon to be before the Chamber, to us, from the Prosecution's perspective, should be more reliable than a note of an interview taken by the Croatian police. Nevertheless, we, in particular here with the Gotovina Defence, are in the position where OTP is objecting to the admission of a statement taken by the OTP, which we would seek certification for, on the basis that OTP cannot cross-examination the witness that it, itself, interviewed; while, on the other hand, today coming into court and seeking to tender witness interview notes of the Croatian police, which none of the three defendants can cross-examine. Our broad interest here, Your Honours, is to try to achieve some sort of coherent policy with respect to the admissibility of statements generally. And if the Prosecution believes that statements given to the Croatian MUP that cannot be cross-examined should be admitted, it is our position that the Chamber should take a similar approach with respect to statements taken by OTP, particularly where the Defence is proposing to the follow the procedures outlined in Rule 92 bis. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I first respond to Mr. Misetic's argument. I think the jurisprudence here is very clear; that is, a statement obtained for the purpose of judicial proceedings, the current judicial proceedings, are statements which fall within the scope of 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater; and unless the requirements of those rules are fulfilled, they cannot be admitted. However, a statement which has been obtained or given to national authorities or other agencies, not for purposes of this particular proceedings before court, are admissible. I think that's the current jurisprudence, and, in fact, I can, if necessary, cite the references in the Haradinaj decision and established jurisprudence. So there is a legal basis for the admission of this -- these records of interviews conducted by officials of the Ministry of Interior. Apart from that, Mr. President, there is also a factual basis contrary to what Mr. Cayley said. This witness is in a position and he has already through his supplementary statement identified these notes. Those were interviews conducted pursuant to an investigation initiated by this witness in 2001. And upon his instructions -- upon his instructions, the officials of the Ministry of Interior conducted the interviews and then submitted the interview notes to him, and he has perused each one of them. In fact, in his supplemental statement, he even goes on to say that he identified certain notations and markings on these records of interview made by himself. So there is a factual basis. Apart from which, based on these notes, the witness has made certain indicia to continue with the investigation. So, it is not -- it is material that these statements were made, they were recorded; and based often these notes, the witness has made certain indicia. So there is a factual basis and a legal basis for admissibility. Apart from which, comparison of these statements, particularly if you compare the record of interview between Veselin Karanovic and Marija Djuric, there is consistency on the -- between the versions, which adds to the indicia of reliability. This is a mere matter of whether that goes weight that the Trial Chamber will consider at the appropriate stage. So my submission is there is a legal basis and factual basis for admission of these notes for interview, and they differ substantially from statements obtained by investigators of the OTP or investigators of Defence for purposes of these trial proceedings. With regard to the three press articles addressed by Mr. Cayley, that is, 65 ter 6102 and 6103, they are enclosures to a document that is 65 ter 2572; that is, a memo sent by the current witness to the Sibenik-Knin police administration, instructing them to continue with the investigation. In fact, the witness has enclosed these two articles with that letter and has sent it to the Sibenik-Knin police administration giving them notice that based on those press articles that they are to take certain investigative steps. Now, the Defence has not objected to the letter; that is, 2572. It is included in the 92 ter submission. These two press articles are, in fact, enclosures. If you take away the attachments, the letter itself is incomplete, so it does not make any sense to keep away the two press clippings. Apart from which, the relevance of the press clippings is that during the particular time is the fact that the crimes had occurred had been published in newspapers, which goes to the issue of notice. So Mr. Cayley's arguments on the inability to cross-examine the journalist who wrote the press articles doesn't apply any longer, because it is a matter that these incidents have been openly published and, as such, is relevant and has probative value. I have nothing further to add, Mr. President, unless there is any particular issue you want me to address. Mr. President, may I also add - I'm sorry for going back - the Defence itself has admitted records of interviews made by MUP officials, and if I just give a couple of examples: D902, an Official Note of interview with Nikola Vucinovic, recorded by Zadar-Knin crime police department; and D8904, the Official Note of interview of David Marincic, by the Zadar-Knin crime police department. These are not witness who were here for any part to cross-examination, and the Defence itself has tendered those notes, so, obviously, the Defence itself acknowledges the admissibility of records of interview made by the Ministry of Interior officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if I did not misunderstand the Defence, the issue is that under no circumstances, an Official Note of an interview could be admitted into evidence, but that the main two issues being the first one if they go to the act and conduct of the accumulative. Even if they would perhaps not literally fall within the frame of Rule 92 bis, that would be a reason not to admit them. The second one is that there is no -- that the witness cannot be cross-examined. Now, of course, admission and the need for cross-examination are not absolutely values. If the other party does not find a reason to cross-examine the witness or if it is about the matter which is dealt with in other evidence, then, of course, is not whether you can admit OTP Official Notes or not. The issue is whether, under the present circumstances, in view of what the Defence has argued, whether these are admissible exhibits. I think that's the issue; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with regard to -- I would say that that is not an issue on which admissibility is dependant on. That is a matter that Court will -- which goes to the weight of the documents and not admissibility. Apart from which, the Prosecution wants to tender these notes to establish that these statements were, in fact, made at that particular time; and based on which, this witness has taken certain steps to continue with the investigation. When weighing the -- the truthfulness of the contents of the documents, the Trial Chamber will have other material which may corroborate or may contradict, and the Trial Chamber will have the opportunity to consider the truthfulness of the contents. For example, one of the press articles that I wish to tender, in fact, corroborates one of the Official Notes to which the Cermak Defence objected. For example, the interview note of Journalist Nada Surjak is fully corroborated by the press article to which also the Cermak Defence has objected. So these matters are matters the Trial Chamber will consider under -- when considering weight to be given to these notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that the Defence would come up with the argument that if one evidentiary element is non-admissible, that the fact that another non-admissible element of evidence would corroborate that, then that would not be of great help to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I would say that the press article is clearly admissible because, in fact, the Defence has tendered several press articles. I think, in fact, it was in Mr. Cermak's Defence that started tendering numerous articles, but I don't want to split hairs here, Mr. President. I just want to point out that the press articles indicate that contemporaneously these incidents were published. Now, just on that basis, they're admissible, so the press articles are admissible items of evidence. My point is that an admissible item of evidence, in fact, corroborates these admissible notes, and, therefore, the issue argued by Cermak Defence is without merit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you say that since you're so confident that the Chamber will reject the objection raised against the press articles, that under those circumstances you can invoke the press articles as corroboration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I didn't quite say that, Mr. President. I'm never confident about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say they're clearly admissible, where the Defence argues that they're not, so that shows at least some confidence in the argument of this debate, and you anticipate already on that. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if I might just briefly address the comments of my learned friend. The MUP Official Notes that are partly the subject of this application are not formal investigative steps. They are not part of the formal judicial investigation that would have taken place in the Republic of Croatia. They are, in fact, part of the stage related to preliminary inquiries in the case. My understanding of Croatian law - and I think that Mikulicic will be asking the witness about this - is that these are notes taken by the police submitted to the public prosecutor, who would then submit those to the investigative magistrate who would be the individual who would take formal statements from these witnesses. So, in terms of their status within Croatian proceedings, they are very low, indeed; and you will see, in our motions, they are not admissible as evidence in proceedings in the Republic of Croatia. I know, respectfully, the Court is not bound by the law of other states, but I do respectfully submit that it is a matter that you should consider when deciding whether or not these particular matters are -- these particular notes are admissible. My learned friend also made the point that reliability goes to weight and not to admissibility, and I would respectfully correct her here, that the jurisdiction of this Tribunal identifies essentially a tipping point. I call it a tipping point because yes, it is true that admissibility goes to weight, but there comes a point in time when the indicia of reliability is so low in a document that it essentially ticks, and the particular item in question is no longer admissible particularly, particularly, where it goes to central issues in the case, such as here the acts and the conduct of the accused. I would refer Your Honours to the 2000 Appeals Chamber decision in Kordic and Cerkez, which is cited to in our pleadings. I would also note the decision in the Haradinaj case which was a decision of this Trial Chamber, which examined statements that had been taken by national authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, if I may interrupt you, it is now the second time that you say it: You're right and you're wrong. You're right to the extent that it is Trial Chamber I, and you're wrong to the extent that the panel of Judges in that case, of course, that there is only one overlap with this case, which is certainly a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't suggesting, Your Honour ... [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no -- MR. CAYLEY. [Overlapping speakers] ... decision of this Chamber. It's of another Trial Chamber in another case, in the Haradinaj case, where statements that were taken by national authorities, so not by the Tribunal itself, not by the Office of the Prosecutor, and which did address the acts and the conduct of the accused that were found to be inadmissible. I can read here from that decision at paragraph 11: "The Chamber refused to admit the evidence," these were essentially statements compiled by national authorities, "refused to admit the evidence and held that admitting statements concerning the acts and conduct of the accused given by persons without the possibility to examine them in court would create a high risk of prejudice to the Defence." Your Honours, we assert the same position here. Lastly, my learned friend stated that this witness can admit these documents because he has received them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you started reading, and I'm just trying to find paragraph 11, because circumstances were rather specific there; isn't it? You were quoting a line, a line saying that a similar caution, even it if not 92 ter statements, is appropriate, and that this is of even greater importance - it says "import" - when the sources are anonymous or unclear and when the material itself contains signs that warrant specific signs as to its reliability. I do remember from that case that there was a rather strong suggestion supported by evidence that people were ill treated when they came to police statements where they statements which, of course, is something which at least I have not found here, until this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a distinction that can be made, but you will see in our filings over the weekend that we do suggest to the Court that there are a number of factors which make these particular MUP official documents unreliable. Different, you're absolutely right, Your Honour, to the situation in Haradinaj, but nevertheless unreliable. I won't go through them, I rehearsed them to you in my first argument, but we still maintain that they are unreliable, they can't be tested, and we do respectfully say that the Court should be extremely cautious about admitting them. In fact, we assert that they should be reject. Lastly, the last point I make is simply this: My learned friend stated that this witness can admit these documents because he can identify them because he received them. Well, frankly, I could admit those documents on them because I have received them and I can identify them, but I can't say anything about the content of these documents about what the witness's has actually stated. This particular gentleman, whilst he is the public prosecutor, he was the public prosecutor on this case, he did not attend these witness interviews, and he cannot give evidence to this Court on what was actually said in those interviews. That is all that I wish to say, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the press articles are concerned, Mr. Cayley, where Ms. Mahindaratne says it is not because I think this journalist would know what had happened, but the importance is this type of publications appeared at the time. Therefore, it seems to me that the evidentiary -- the probative value, rather, is in the fact that these stories were published, rather than to the truth of their contents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, if the Prosecution is saying that that is the only reason that these documents are being admitted, that is one thing; but these documents do contain suggestions, assertions about the acts and content of Mr. Cermak. I do believe that my learned friend was talking about corroboration of these sources by other evidence that is before the Court. On that basis, particularly bearing in mind that there is journalistic comment, particularly bearing in mind that it is very, very difficult to identify the sources of these stories, we would still object to those newspaper articles because we cannot cross-examine this witness on acts and conduct. Notice, I accept, is another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, just briefly in response on the 92 bis issue. Ms. Mahindaratne attempts to make the distinction that the statements taken by OTP were taken for purposes of this proceeding and, therefore, they are inadmissible because Rule 92 bis requirements have not been fulfilled. That seems to be a rather circular argument, Your Honour, because the fact of the matter is we have asked for the Rule 92 bis requirements to be fulfilled, and the Office of the Prosecutor is objecting to allowing us to fulfil the Rule 92 bis retirements, on the basis that the statements are not subject to cross-examination by the Prosecution and are otherwise not reliable. So it is a rather circular argument to say that that is what the distinction is between OTP statements and statements given to the Croatian police. The OTP's position in objecting to 92 bis application is precisely that, A, they cannot cross-examine the statement given to them; and, B, that this witness in the 92 bis filing was not disclosed by the Defence and under Rule 65. Well, those two issues are at play here; similarly, they are now trying to tender statements, albeit given to the Croatian police, that, A, are not subject to cross-examination by the Defence, and, B, involving witnesses who were not disclosed pursuant to Rule 65 ter So I would suggest, Your Honour, that the Prosecution is attempting to have it both ways here. More broadly, and just as a matter of policy and for guidance from the Trial Chamber, on this issue that the -- any statement given to a party in these proceedings, that statement is inadmissible, per se, unless the requirements of 92 bis and Rule 92 -- and/or Rule 92 ter are fulfilled. I would suggest that, Your Honour, that is an artificial distinction being created. While I completely understand that principle with respect to statements taken by a party and then being tendered by that party into evidence, there is an clear policy that would not support such a practice by either the Prosecution or Defence. We are in a different situation here and one that, perhaps, I might suggest was not contemplated by Rule 92 bis or Rule 92 ter, which is that statement taken by the opposing party, where the opposing party was the one who had the opportunity to interview the witness and to record what it is that that witness said in the interview, should indicate that that statement is at least as reliable for the Trial Chamber as a statement given to a third party; in this case, the Croatian police. And what I am -- would particularly seek some clarification or guidance on is the fact that what is the real policy distinction or the real issue of reliability if in fact a statement given to -- between a statement given to an opposing party within these proceedings and where we are attempting to fulfil the requirements of Rule 92 bis, why that statement should be deemed less reliable than a statement given to a non-party where the requirements of neither Rule 92 bis or Rule 92 ter are being fulfilled. I would suggest, Your Honour, that these are artificial distinctions that the Prosecution, in light of the arguments that it raised in opposition to our Rule 92 bis filing, should either be required to allow statements in -- in cross-examination if in fact the requirements of the rules are fulfilled; or, if not, then should not be allowed to tender witness statements of non-parties into evidence, because the principles should be the same, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the argument that you can't have the cake and eat it, could you please respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is, needless to say, that 92 bis is a -- 92 bis, 92 quater is -- they are exceptional situations; that is, unless the conditions are fulfilled for a 92 bis admission, they would not admitted. Now, in the same vein, where the Prosecution attempts to tender statements under 92 bis, the Defence would object if the Defence is of the view that we have not fulfilled the particular criteria that is required for admission of a statement under 92 bis. And, likewise, in the given situation, the Defence attempted to admit a statement where the Prosecution was of the view that the -- the witness could be brought to court and be subject to cross-examination, and unless the specific conditions have been fulfilled, you know, we had the right to object and I think the final decision as to whether it was a matter which warrants a statement to be admitted under 92 bis will be determined by Court. So the fact that we objected to that given situation where the Defence attempted to admit a statement under 92 bis does not in any way contradict what I stated earlier with regard to the fact that statements which fall within the scope of 92 bis, 92 quater, and 92 ter, unless the criteria is fulfilled, would not be allowed to be admitted, as opposed to statements which fall outside that scope. I don't think the Prosecution was trying to have the cake and eat it, contrary to what Mr. Misetic stated. It is just that in that given scenario the Prosecution was satisfied that it had a basis to file an objection because we were of the view that the Defence had not fulfilled, or the situation had not -- was not of a -- the required conditions which would permit admission under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I must admit that I have missed the response by the Prosecution against this matter and, of course, it is now put into play, so to say. So, therefore, I -- there was a lot of material filed, whereas I usually and my colleagues are very often very much available over the weekend. That's not the same for every weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not get you. Did you say when you said you missed the response with regard to the 92 bis objection or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My response now or the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Your response now, it was clear and well understood what you said, but the written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We did not file written submissions, Mr. President, but with regard to the 92 bis, I could get the objections to Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think, as a matter of fact, someone said had been filed over the weekend. So, therefore, this could also have been perhaps an a courtesy copy already given. Yes, but I hope the parties will understand that if the courtesy copies are flying over in the weekend and if the Chamber is not receiving copies, usually we wait until a matter is filed unless we have a specific reason to expect that something comes in, in which case we often ask for a courtesy copy. My recollection is that the -- that we asked when a response would be filed, and I think the answer we got at that time, that it would be on Friday. Ms. Mahindaratne, on the 92 bis. I think I specifically asked for that because we saw that there was some urgency in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can advise you that the OTP did in fact file it Friday evening and serve courtesy copies on the parties and the Chamber on Friday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, nevertheless then, I have missed that -- those written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to take much more of your time or go over the same grounds again. However, the exchange of arguments between the OTP and the Defence teams somehow implies that we're talking about witness statements. However, I repeat, Official Notes compiled by the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia are not witness statements because they're not signed and they don't contain any information to the witness about their right and obligations. This is simply a piece of paper produced by the MUP after an interview with a certain person, X/Y. Thus, this is not a statement, and such a piece of paper, especially in the absence of the person who -- from whom the -- that piece of paper originated, cannot be subject to Rules 92, bis, or ter, or whatever other rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is clear if there is no attestation from those person that they cannot be introduced or admitted under Rule 92 ter. But that seems not to be the primary issue. The issue primarily seems to be whether there other avenues through which the statements and then for what purposes they could be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just add one thing, just in response to what Mr. Cayley said, just a minor -- just a correction. This witness did not merely receive, and I said this before but I -- just so -- just to respond to Mr. Cayley. These notes were obtained, recorded pursuant to the witness's instructions. He was directing the investigation. I just wanted to point out that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you said that out already, but at least -- and if so, it is now twice on the record. This is now twice on the record as well, the evidentiary status of these documents, under Croatian law. The Chamber will need some time to consider both the written submissions and an oral argument that has been made this morning. It is difficult to forecast time we would need. The parties are invited to remain stand by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that there was a technical problem as well, with moving from one kind of session into other kind of session, a matter which needs the urgent attention of our technicians. Therefore, under those circumstances, and which -- just looking at the clock, if we would restart at 10.30, so then we have a relatively long break now, and that with one other short break, we might come through this morning. Therefore, the parties are invited to remain stand by, well, let's say, on from 25 minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the various matters, and gives guidance to the parties as follows. On the admission of the exhibits which were objected, the Chamber gives a final decision on one only at this stage. The Chamber will not admit into evidence the Official Note compiled on the 10th of January, 2002, which relates to an interview conducted in the Zagreb police administration on the 9th of January 2002 of, well, let's say, the interview given by Mr. Cermak. As far as the other exhibits are concerned, the Chamber invites the parties to have them marked for identification if there's any objection against any of these documents, because the Chamber has difficulties at this moment, where the witness is still available, to finally assess whether any reliability concerns are opposing admission. So, therefore, we'll take advantage of the availability of this witness, and at the very end, we'll decide on the admission. Then there was another matter that is about a 92 bis submission made by the Defence opposed by the Prosecution. At this moment, the Chamber is struggling with the stage of the proceedings, and we'll still have to finally make up our mind whether or not this is an appropriate way of proceeding. That's an element which is entirely apart from the other matter raised therein, that is, the strict 92 bis requirements, and whether the position taken by Prosecution, what consequences that should have finally for the decision to be taken on the admission of exhibits, specialty the Official Notes that were or at least that will be tendered and provisionally marked for identification. At least, Ms. Mahindaratne, where you said you withdraw one, I take it that then you will tender the others. We'll see that in the context of the respective submissions from both parties, and then take them into consideration. But the timing, at this stage of the proceedings, of course, is a matter which is rather separate from that, and, therefore, the Chamber is not in a position yet to decide on that matter. But, of course, we'll have to do that soon because the witness, through which this 92 bis material would be introduced, is on the list rather soon. So, therefore, if this may guide the parties on how to proceed in the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, then the Chamber will finally decide on the matter. Then the reasons for already now deciding not to admit the Official Note in relation to the, if I could say, the Cermak interview, those will be given at a later stage. That needs some careful formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note you didn't mention anything about the articles. Is that included?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Articles are included, yes, at the same level. Also, we'll deal with them, you can put questions about them. There are many elements in those articles as we have discussed before the break, such as, that it was published, what was published. Apparently, there is also mentioning of what supposedly had been said by the accused. So, therefore, that will be dealt with in a similar way. At the same time, just to give an example, there is corroboration about many days of rain, for example. That is a relatively neutral element in the whole of it, but, of course, it's a complex matter, and we'll finally decide on whether it goes to weight or whether it goes to admission. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to call your the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Mr. Zeljko Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, yes. No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zganjer. I hope that I pronounced your name in the right way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which also confirms that you can hear me in a language you understand. Mr. Zganjer, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zganjer. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, I saw that you took some documents out of your bag. If during your examination you would feel any need to consult any document, would you please tell me so that it's clear when you are and when you're not consulting your documents. Mr. Zganjer, you will first be examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Zeljko Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: At this moment, I am a lawyer in Zagreb; I have my own private office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On 8th December 2005 and 12th July 2006, were you interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. November 2008 and July 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How about 8 December 2005, Mr. Zganjer? Do you recall being interviewed in 2005, December?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of those two interviews when the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor asked you questions, did you answer them truthfully?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: I answered truthfully and to the extent of my recollection of the details involved. I was asked questions about the circumstances of some things that happened five or six years before, perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were those two interviews audio-recorded?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes, tape-recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you meet with members of the Office of the Prosecutor on 4th and 5th November 2008?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you provided with audiotapes and the corresponding transcripts of those tapes in advance of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At that meeting --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to clarify something. I was provided with the tapes of my interview. During the actual interview, on the 8th and 9th of November this year, I was given an addendum to my previous interview with the ICTY investigators which was something that had not been forwarded to me via e-mail. I looked at the addendum, and I have had a chance to familiarize myself with its substance before coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, I was going to ask you about the addendum which is the supplementary statement, if you would allow me. At that meeting - you referred to "addendum," and we use the term "supplementary statement" here - at that meeting, did you provide a supplementary statement to the Office of the Prosecutor; that is, on the 4th and 5th of November, 2008?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes. I supplemented my statement, and I explained some things during my interview with the Prosecutor on the 8th and 9th of November, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I was getting to that, Mr. Zganjer. I don't intend to in any event not to lead that evidence, so if you just allow me. Now, at that meeting, did you inform the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor that you had reviewed the transcripts of your previous two interviews and that you made -- wanted to make a clarification. Subject to that clarification, subject the contents of the transcripts were accurate and true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: That's true. What you suggest is true. There were clarifications, and the transcript of my interview was made to reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And last evening, or perhaps this morning, did you have the opportunity to examine your supplementary statement that you gave on the 4th and 5th November?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did the supplementary statement accurately reflect what you had stated to the members of the Office of the Prosecutor on 4th and 5th November?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes, it did. There were some additional explanations that were furnished, which I believe resulted in a greater degree of precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are the contents of the supplementary statement true, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Indeed, true to the extent that I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you were asked the questions that were asked of you by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on 8th December 2005, that is, December 2005 interview; on 12th July 2006; and on 4th and 5th November 2008, today here in court, would your responses be the same? When I say "same," one would not expect it to be verbatim, but would the substance be the same?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt. I believe it would be essentially all the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to move into evidence the -- the tapes and the transcripts of the two interviews, and I refer to them by the 65 ter number and the supplementary statement. The first interview, that is, the interview of 8 December 2005, is under 65 ter 6083, and that includes four transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against admission of 6083.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1046.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1046 is admitted into evidence. The next one would be, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 65 ter 6084, and that's the interview on 12th July 2006. That includes five transcripts. Mr. President, I want to clarify the record. There are six tapes but only five transcripts. They capture all six, and let me explain. The tape bearing ERN number T0005443 has side A and B, and there are corresponding transcripts to that; then there are two tapes bearing ERN T0005444, which has side A and B. There are two transcripts corresponding to those two tapes. Then there are two final tapes, T0005445, side A and B; but there is only one transcript which captured both tapes. So, hence, the five transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. No objections against 6084. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1047.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1047 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could call on the screen, Mr. Registrar, 6105; that is, the supplementary statement of 4th and 5th November.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, in a moment, you'll see on your screen a statement, and if you could just look at it. Is this the first page --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We will wait for the B/C/S document to come up, and, Mr. Registrar, if you could go to the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, is that the cover page of your supplementary statement provided on 4th and 5th November, 2008?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we move to the not the last page, but one before the last page, and if we could ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, do you recognise your signature at the bottom of the page, under the declaration, if you could wait for the B/C/S to come up. Is that your statement that you just saw?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Indeed, that is my signature. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to move into evidence a supplement statement, dated 4th and 5th November 2008, 65 ter 6105.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Registrar, 6105 would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1048, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1048 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Mahindaratne, in view of the earlier guidance or ruling, may I take it that documents you want to tender from the bar table, of course, perhaps in relation with the remainder of the testimony of the witness, that you would usually have it tendered, but that we already know that if you would give that information at this moment, that everything would be marked for identification for the time being. Documents you will specifically deal with, of course, will get immediately an MFI number; whereas, the others will have to wait until a final list has been produced. I'm talking about the very practical matter of numbering.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's anything would you like to raise with the witness during the examination-in-chief, I suggest that it will be given the MFI number immediately, and whatever then remains, if there is anything to be tendered from the bar table, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I have already tendered 19 documents from the bar table of which I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But usually some documents are nevertheless dealt with. I don't know whether that is it your intention or not. Then sometimes that list becomes shorter. Then, of course, what then remains is for the registrar to provisionally assign numbers; that is, to give them MFI numbers to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll keep that in mind. Whenever I deal with a document in the bar table submission, I will inform the Court of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Zganjer, I have to -- Mr. Zganjer, you're looking at Ms. Mahindaratne, but I'm speaking to you at this moment. Mr. Zganjer, this is also perhaps a good moment to explain to you why you had to wait for a while. There were some procedural aspects of documents you had been referring to, which were raised last Friday and over the weekend and which were further discussed this mourning in court, and the Chamber had to take some time to give a ruling and or to give guidance on these matters. So that is why you had to wait for such a long time before you were invited to enter the courtroom, just for you to you know. Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One other thing, Mr. President, the Prosecution filed a motion to add three documents, that is, 65 ter 6102 and 6103, in relation to which there is an objection regarding admissibility, but this is with regard to the motion to add, as well as 6088. Mr. President, they are documents which were not in the 65 ter list, if I could have a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, only that standing objection that we've made in respect of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which will finally materialise in our decision on admission, rather than on being added to the 65 ter list; is that how I have to understand it? Then leave is granted, Ms. Mahindaratne, to add them to the 65 ter list, but this is not a decision yet on admission into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I read a summary of the witness's testimony at this stage, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained to the witness the purpose of this, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zeljko Zganjer was the deputy to the head state attorney of the Republic of Croatia from February 2003 to February 2006. During the period relevant to the indictment, and until September 2002, he served as a county state attorney for Sibenik. Mr. Zganjer provides information relating to the structure and workings of the law enforcement and judicial system in Croatia. His evidence covers the procedure followed by the military and civilian police to investigate crimes, the involvement and role of the state prosecutor and the investigating judge in such investigations, and the procedure relating to the processing of crime. The witness provides information concerning the investigations and prosecutions undertaken by the Croatian authorities with respect to crimes committed during and in the aftermath Operation Storm. The witness was directly involved in, amongst others, the investigation of the killing incidents in Gosic and Varivode. In 2001, the witness initiated an investigation into the incident in Grubori which occurred on 25th August 1995. That is all, Mr. President. I could move on with the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I have permission of Court to hand over the binder of hard copies of his statement and transcripts to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is usual practice, so since I hear of no objections, you may hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, let me just explain, so that there won't be any interruptions when you move. The binder right at the top has your supplementary statement given in November, and thereafter the interview notes are attached with tab markings which indicate which interview notes are enclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document 2572, please. Mr. President, this is a document which was included in the 92 ter motion, but in view of the guidelines with regard to documentation received today, I'm calling it up right now. So, Mr. Registrar, if you could take a note of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, if I could just take you to paragraph 13 of your supplementary statement. Mr. Zganjer, before you go to the document, if I could ask you to look at paragraph 13. At paragraph 13, for the record, P1048, you state that you're shown a memo, dated 31st May 2001, which you say: "... which I sent to the Sibenik-Knin crime police department. The memo concerns the killings in Grubori in August 1995, and also attaches media articles relating to these events." And you refer to the memo -- the reference number of the memo. Is that the memo you referred to in paragraph 13?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes, that is the memo. If I may just make one observation, paragraph 13 talks about the 31st of March 2001; whereas, the memo that I'm looking at on my screen bears the date the 31st of May, if I'm not mistaken 2001. Nevertheless, the substance of the memo is consistent with the one that I was thinking of. I do notice that one discrepancy concerning the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Zganjer, it must be a translation error in the Croatian version of the statement, because in the English statement which you have signed, the date is correctly recorded as 31st May 2001. Moving on, you have attached two media articles and sent it to the Sibenik-Knin police administration, and you go on to say this, and I'm reading paragraph 2 of the document which is on the screen: "For the purposes of the criminal investigation processing, I am enclosing copies of articles published in the newspaper Slobodna Dalmacija," pardon my pronunciation, "on 25th, 26th, and 29th August 1995, entitled 'Mopping-up operation: Five Chetniks killed and Reaper with a machine-gun,' which discussed the incident in Grubori hamlet in detail." Then in the next paragraph, you go on to say: "In addition to the persons referred to in the article, 'Reaper with a machine-gun,' interviews also need to be conducted with citizens Draginja Djuric and Marija Djuric, who, according to information gathered, have some knowledge of the incident." In the next paragraph, you say: "I reiterate may insistence that all measures and actions set out in the aforesaid request be implemented as a matter of urgency." Now, what was the reason which led to you to send these press articles to the Sibenik-Knin police administration? Why did you consider that relevant to the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Any information on an incident that the state prosecutor happens to be looking into might prove helpful in what we refer to as pre-trial investigations. We work on collecting the evidence of any crimes and their potential perpetrators. It is in that light that the media articles should be viewed. Again, as I said in the memo, these focussed on the incident in Grubori. As far as I can now remember, actual names were given in those media articles, names of citizens who knew something about what had happened. Therefore, in my assessment, these articles were useful, or potentially useful, in terms of helping us find out a number of things that at a later stage in the proceedings might have proved helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... regards to the translation, Your Honour. Again, it seems that we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, if there is a problem, you know how to resolve that. We invite then the witness to repeat a portion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask specific attention of the interpreters for that portion, and then if anything remains, then we'll ask the witness to take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of it, Your Honour. What I'm referring to is a statement of the witness, which was put into the transcript under page 37 and line 10. It relates to the part of the proceedings which has been translated as a "pre-trial investigation." That kind of translation is something that is not accurate to the what witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask the witness to repeat what he said, and then if there's any discussion, so that we first try to avoid whatever mistake, and if then there's another matter remaining, then we'll look at that. If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Page 37, line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I see what most likely the issue may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean, this is specific to the Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's follow the order I suggested, that is, that we first exclude for any possibility that there is a mistake, and then if there's any legal matter to be discussed, that we can do it. Your answer was, and I now read it in English: "Any information on an incident that the state prosecutor happens to be looking into might prove helpful in what we refer to as ..." Then could you repeat what you then said? Because may I take it that that is the issue, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought it would be. So what you referred to as what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was very specific. I said that, at this stage, we were dealing with pre-criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think this type of translation, as we are facing now in the transcript, is more accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently, what I understand your request for clarification is such, Mr. Mikulicic, that you would say we have not yet entered the stage where criminal proceedings have started, but have not yet reached the trial stage, but this is a kind of an introduction to what may become criminal investigation, criminal proceedings. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is precisely what I had in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I tender that document into evidence, Mr. President. As I said, it is already included in the 92 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1049.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1049 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may have I document number 6103, please. And, Mr. President, for the record, two articles referred to in the previous document, that is, P1049, have been included, but we have not been able to secure the third article. I just wanted to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, these, at least all three of them, were attached to the letter. Do you now keep them separate as you did before, that is, that the articles are appear on your bar table list; or do you consider the two newspaper articles to be attached and to be part of P1049?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is so, Mr. President, as attachments to P1049.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And they have been uploaded as such into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. At the moment, this is pursuant to the objection, so we have to adjust it. Accordingly, at the moment, they are separate documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly why I was asking. I said P1049 is admitted into evidence, and, of course, this would not include in accordance with the ruling I gave earlier or the guidance I gave earlier. So what we have to do now is to have MFI numbers for the two articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That is why, although they are referred to in P1049, I would bring them up and deal with the witness, so that the Trial Chamber would have relevant testimony required for assessment of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I do not know what specific questions you would like to put to the witness in relation it this press articles. Perhaps, apart from that these were the ones, I don't know whether that's a matter which could be agreed upon by the parties. I'm just wondering what exercise we're now engaging in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I mean, if simply I think the point you're make is if the witness received these documents, or if the witness transmitted these document to the police, we don't disagree with that. I mean, I think we can move very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that is not an issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if that's the only point, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to put further questions, then, of course, Ms. Mahindaratne, we'll have to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have one further question. If I could have on the English translation, Mr. Registrar, number 06436582. That is the cover page, the caption under photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zganjer, while that is being done, you could obviously follow the B/C/S document. Under that photograph of Mr. Cermak and another person, it reads --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could, Mr. Registrar, focus on that caption just below the photograph. I wonder if it could be brought up further so that the witness could read that small caption under the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, are you able to read that caption under the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And it reads: "'If I had wronged Croatian, I would have fled like the others did,' Veselin Karanovic explains to General Cermak in Grubori." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Is that correct," Ms. Mahindaratne, is not a very --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to ask the witness that, unless there is a translation issue. Please put --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have one question relevant question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Come with relate question --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just for the purpose of the record. I mean, you know what I'm go to say, Your Honour. She can't ask questions -- asking the witness to simply read this article, trying to establish the truth of the document, it's not a proper exercise, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that was not the objective at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be clear. If we have an original and a translation in which there is text, then there is no need to ask a witness whether that is what the document reads.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I was just creating sort of a preliminary question for the required -- the question that I want to ask, which is relevant. It is not in any way an inappropriate exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then first put that question to the witness. And, Mr. Zganjer, I would like you to perhaps wait a second with answering the question, so that if there would be any objection, that it can be raised before you answer that question. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the course of the investigation initiated by you in 2001, did the Sibenik-Knin crime police interview Veselin Karanovic and submit the official record of that interview to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, I think there was no Official Note reflecting an interview with Veselin Karanovic. I don't think a record of that interview was ever submitted to me, again to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one point. I'm not objecting to that question, but I'm just objecting to the characterization. I think Mr. Mikulicic has already stated this. My learned friend is using the term "investigation," and this was not an investigation under Croatian law. The investigation would have started at the point in time when the investigative magistrate took matters up. This was actually prior to the formal investigation, as far as I understand Croatian law. So I would just ask that the questions be characterised in that fashion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you're invited to express yourself as precise as possible. On the other hand, there is no need to further intervene if anyone makes a mistake, because if ever -- the Chamber is now fully aware that it should clearly distinguish between all the different stages of any efforts to find out the truth about matters that have been reported and which may have a criminal implication, and this is the general term for a very general, very general phenomenon which is often referred to as an investigation at its different stages. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, is it possible that you probably have forgotten. Let me take you to paragraph 18 of your supplementary statement, where you did, in fact, examine Mr. Karanovic's official record of interview.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. This note obviously exists in the file. It was shown to me. I'm sure that I had it before me during this interview, and I confirm that that was one of the notes that I had received during the pre-criminal proceedings by the police. That's why I would like to correct my previous statement, or, rather, what I said just a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I move this into evidence, and I do note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking for it to be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1050, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it keeps that status. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I will just, from the bar table, Mr. President, tender 65 ter 6102, which is the other media article. Mr. Registrar, if could you bring it up and give it a numbering, an MFI numbering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check to see what we have. Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1051, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could have document number 6085, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, let me, in fairness to you, since you forgot, let me just bring up Mr. Karanovic's statement, so that you can examine it and which you referred to at paragraph 13 -- sorry, 18 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, I don't mean to intervene, but it keeps getting called a "statement." It is not a statement. It is an Official Note, and I think we need to be precise here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The official record of interview --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely the Official Note recorded after the interview with Citizen Karanovic. You showed it to me either on the 8th or 9th of November of this year during my interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That was 4th and 5th, Mr. Zganjer. I just wanted to correct the record.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: Very well. The 4th or the 5th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you know what led to the criminal police to interview Mr. Karanovic? Was it pursuant to your instructions or what was the factor that led them to interview him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: It was very obvious; the reasons were quite clear. Veselin Karanovic resided in the territory at the time, at the moment when this incident occurred. The mere fact pointed to a possibility that he might have certain information about the events that were subject of my interest, as well as the subject of the police operations after the incident that had taken place in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell Court as to what procedure or what methods did the police follow in conducting these interviews? To start off, where were these interviews conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER
utterances.text: I personally was not present during that interview. I can't tell you whether that interview was conducted on the premises of the police administration of the county of Sibenik and Knin, or that maybe it was conducted at the place of residence of Citizen Veselin Karanovic who was interviewed. As I look at the Official Note on the screen, I can't see where the interview actually took place, but I allow that it may have been one of the locations that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how do those Official Notes assist you in your investigation? Did you consider these notes as usual for your investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to object to the question as being pretty leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At page 47 line 3, the question was: "... these notes as useful for your investigation," and that's what I'm objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I started off by saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course, we could ask, "Did you consider them useful or not useful." Of course, a question has to focus on something and it's not on whether the witness liked the typewriting of it or whether he preferred long or short ones. I mean, these are all questions in relation to that. So we have to focus one way or the other, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Could you please tell us whether you consider these Official Note useful or not useful for the work you had to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to clarify one thing. This Official Note that we have in the file, according to the Croatian penal code and according to the rules of the criminal procedure, is not evidence. It is just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no doubt. It's not the subject of the question to you, that whether it is evidence or not. The question was whether it helped you in performing your duties, and not whether it could be used in evidence in court at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, it was useful in this pre-criminal proceedings. It was a piece of information provided by Mr. Karanovic as to what he knew and what he might tell us in the criminal proceedings against perpetrators, i.e., what he might be able to provide as a witness in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may this document be tendered into evidence. This is again a document included in the bar table motion. Mr. Registrar, if you would take note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Subject to the MFI -- these are MFIs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1052, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it keeps that status for the time being. Could I ask one additional question. Did those Official Notes also provide information which you could us in giving instructions for further investigations, further - I hardly dare to use the word "investigations" - but how to proceed in your pre-criminal investigations? Did these Official Notes help to you find your way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, the contents of these notes might help a state attorney in his further proceedings in the pre-criminal proceedings. It all depends on the type of information and its significance that a citizen offers during his interview with the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that, or I ask you, could that trigger, for example, new areas of investigation? On the basis of this information, would you use that, if of course relevant, to explore matters dealt with in such Official Notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, Your Honours, I don't know what Citizen Karanovic said. But if Citizen Karanovic had said that there was a witness in the village by the name X/Y who had been an eye-witness to the events, then the words in his statement would prompt me as a state attorney to order the police to conduct an interview with the possible witness mentioned by Citizen Karanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And, Mr. Registrar, if could I just call up 65 ter 1166.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zganjer, in fact, I didn't go according to the sequence. I should have shown you this document first. This is the document sent to you by the Sibenik-Knin crime police department on 16th July 2001. It reads as follows, and I'm reading the first paragraph. It says: "Further to your request and the documents sent to us, please be informed that, to date, we have interviewed the following persons: Draginja Djuric, Marija Djuric, and Veselin Karanovic.
